The FOMC’s decision to hold the target range at 5.25–5.50% while continuing balance-sheet runoff signals a rule-like, forecast-based stance consistent with the modern monetary policy literature: estimates of U.S. policy behavior (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler) and inflation-forecast targeting frameworks (Svensson and Woodford) emphasize waiting for sufficient evidence that inflation is on a sustained path to 2%. The emphasis on “greater confidence” before cutting is also consistent with time-inconsistency and inflation-bias concerns in the literature, reinforcing the value of credibility and expectations anchoring in New Keynesian models (via the Phillips curve). With unemployment still low (limited slack per Okun’s law) and inflation “elevated” despite easing, Taylor-rule prescriptions argue for a still-restrictive stance. Operationally, interest on reserves and standing facilities support rate control in the floor system, while ongoing QT likely nudges term premia higher at the margin. The “risks … moving into better balance” softens the hawkish tone versus 2023, but the net message remains cautiously positive growth with inflation vigilance.
